Introduction

[
1
]

Eastern Platinum Ltd. (“EPL”) is a publicly
traded company incorporated in BC. As its name suggests, it is involved in the
platinum mining business and indirectly owns a mine in South Africa, known as
the Crocodile River Mine. Its shares are publicly traded on the Toronto and Johannesburg
stock exchanges.

[
2
]

The plaintiff Mr.
Rong
Kai
Hong represents himself and 2538520 Ontario Limited (“253 Ont. Ltd.”)
in all three proceedings before me, although prior to November 2024, both Mr. Hong
and 253 Ont. Ltd. were represented by counsel.

[
3
]

The core events giving rise to these proceedings
occurred more than a decade ago and relate to an unsuccessful bid by Mr. Hong
to acquire a controlling stake in EPL in 2015 and 2016. Instead, another company,
Ka An Development Co. Ltd. (“Ka An”), acquired the controlling stake, and after
a proxy battle, elected its slate of directors to the board of directors at EPL’s
Annual General Meeting on July 5, 2016.

[
4
]

Mr. Hong was not a shareholder of EPL at
the time of this proxy battle and admits that he has never personally held
shares in EPL. He also admits that he incorporated 253 Ont. Ltd. in September
2016. In 2017, 253 Ont. Ltd. acquired a minority shareholding position in EPL.

[
5
]

The claims also relate to a proposal that Mr. Hong
made to EPL’s directors in 2018, for EPL to explore a deal involving chrome
offtake from the Crocodile River Mine. These overtures were rebuffed and,
instead, EPL entered into a deal with a third party, Union Goal (the “Union
Goal Transaction” or “Union Goal Transactions”). Mr. Hong maintains that
the Union Goal Transaction was improvident and resulted from undisclosed
conflicts of interest between Union Goal, Ka An, and EPL’s directors and
officers.

[
6
]

After EPL’s transaction with Union Goal in 2018,
Mr. Hong and/or 253 Ont. Ltd. commenced five separate proceedings against
EPL and the related defendants: one in Ontario and four in this jurisdiction.

[
7
]

In the first of the BC proceedings, 253 Ont. Ltd.
sought leave to commence a derivative action over the 2018 Union Goal Transaction.
Justice N. Smith denied leave on the basis Mr. Hong was not acting in good
faith in bringing the action:
2538520 Ontario Ltd. v. Eastern Platinum
Limited,
2019 BCSC 1446
, aff’d
2020 BCCA 313
.

[
8
]

An additional and separate derivative proceeding
was commenced by a shareholder of EPL, after Mr. Hong issued a press
release—following the dismissal of the first derivative action—inviting
shareholders to seek leave to pursue a similar derivative action. That action
is ongoing.

[
9
]

The applications now before me concern the three
remaining BC proceedings, all of which were commenced while the appeal of N. Smith
J.’s decision denying leave for the derivative action was underway. Certain of
the defendants seek to strike the plaintiffs’ claims under either R. 9-6 as
disclosing no genuine issue for trial or under Subrules 9-5(1)(a)–(d) of the
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
.

[
10
]

The defendants submit that all three claims suffer from multiple
obvious and fatal flaws. Chief among these are that Mr. Hong and 253 Ont. Ltd.
lack standing to seek an oppression remedy, that their claims are derivative and
require leave of the court, and that the pleadings disclose no reasonable cause
of action.

[
11
]

The defendants also submit that the proceedings are an abuse of
process because, at their core, they constitute a continuation of Mr. Hong’s
campaign to seek retribution for his failed bid to gain control of EPL and to
relitigate issues that have previously been adjudicated.

[
12
]

Mr. Hong opposes the applications and submits that there are numerous
triable issues that must be resolved on their merits at trial. He further
submits that the R. 9-6 motions should be dismissed on the grounds that the
defendants have resisted producing documents and that it would be premature to
dismiss the claims in advance of full discovery. He denies that any of the
proceedings amount to an abuse of process.

Mr. Hong’s Decision to
Self-Represent

[
13
]

Up until February 2024, Mr. Hong and 253
Ont. Ltd. were represented by counsel. Thereafter, Mr. Hong advised the
parties that he intended to act on behalf of both himself and the corporate
plaintiff. This led to an application before Justice Kirchner to compel 253
Ont. Ltd. to retain counsel. In light of the right of all persons to represent
themselves in civil proceedings and following confirmation that 253 Ont. Ltd.
was solely owned by Mr. Hong, Kirchner J. concluded that Mr. Hong should
be permitted to represent 253 Ont. Ltd (the “Kirchner J. Decision”). In reasons
indexed at
2025 BCSC 1096
, Kirchner J. made several findings regarding Mr. Hong’s
litigation conduct. In particular, he stated the following:

[43]      Nor

am

I

persuaded

that

it

is

“proper”

for

Mr. Hong

to represent

253

given

his

track
record

thus far in these proceedings.
Mr. Hong has initiated

multiple
and duplicative proceedings. The Oppression Action appears to be the central
vehicle for his and 253’s claims and the Great Wall Action seems

to have been

commenced

to avoid
the need for application to

amend
the notice of civil claim in the Oppression Action.

Both proceedings are

irregular

in

that

oppression

proceedings

are

to

be

commenced

by

petition

rather

than by

notice

of

civil

claim.

This

irregularity

appears

to

be

the

reason

for

the

third

proceeding,
the Great Wall Petition, which duplicates claims in the Great Wall Action. The
multiple proceedings are confusing and likely an

abuse of process

insofar
as

they overlap. This has

undoubtedly

made

it

more

difficult

and

expensive

for

EPL

to

defend

these

proceedings and valuable court time will be needed to sort out and
potentially consolidate

the
proceedings and

perhaps dismiss

those claims that overlap.

It seems these multiple proceedings

have

come

about

because

of

Mr. Hong’s

impatience

in

having

his

application
to amend the notice of civil claim in the Oppression Action heard, which does
not speak well to his capacity to manage these proceedings on behalf of 253.
There is also the problem of Mr. Hong purporting to add defendants to
these proceedings without leave of the court.

[44]      I am also concerned that these
proceedings, like the Derivative Action application that N. Smith J. dismissed,
are further acts of retribution over Mr. Hong’s failed bid to take control
EPL. That was the basis on which N. Smith J. found Mr. Hong lacked the
required good faith to bring the Derivative Action. Equally concerning is the
Court of Appeal’s finding at para. 84 of its reasons dismissing the appeal
from N. Smith J. that Mr. Hong “exaggerated the facts to suit his
interests and advanced allegations of undisclosed conflicts of interests,
without evidence, against the Proposed Defendant Directors.” This raises a
significant question as to whether it is proper that Mr. Hong be permitted
to pursue this case as 253’s representative.

[45]      EPL also points out that Mr. Hong
lacks an understanding of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
and
acts in contravention of them. This adds to EPL’s costs in defending the
actions and the use of scarce and valuable court time is taken up with
correcting his errors and missteps. These include filing multiple claims,
purporting to unilaterally amend claims when leave of the court is required,
and purporting to add parties without leave of the court. EPL also points to Mr. Hong’s
actions which have frustrated EPL’s attempts to have their applications heard
and his selective availably which seems to be flexible when needed to suit his
own needs but not EPL’s.

[46]      In view of all
this – and particularly the fact that I am far from convinced that the cost of
legal counsel would present any financial hardship for Mr. Hong – I would
have been inclined to grant a limited stay of the proceeding so that 253 would
be required to retain counsel at least until the pleadings in the three
proceedings are sorted out and closed. Experienced legal counsel could work to
eliminate those claims that are unnecessary and consolidate those that overlap.
Proper applications to amend and add parties could be brought. Legal counsel,
as an officer of the court, would also have a professional obligation not to
advance a meritless claim that is brought only to seek retribution for Mr. Hong’s
loss in the proxy battle. Once the multiplicity of claims is remedied and the
pleadings closed, it could then be open to Mr. Hong to apply again to
represent 253 if that was his wish.

…

[52]      For
good or bad, Mr. Hong has chosen to represent himself and what he says is
his own company in this proceeding. I certainly do not endorse that as a wise
course of action. The case he is pursuing is factually and legally complex and
the damages he seeks (some $50 million) are significant. With respect, I do not
share Mr. Hong’s confidence in his ability to prosecute these complicated
matters as a self-represented party. He states that he does not want to spend
money on lawyers even though it appears this is not a financial barrier for
him. In my view, he would be well advised to treat the cost of experienced
legal counsel as an investment rather than an expense. However, that is his
choice to make.

[
14
]

I am mindful that as a judge, I have a duty to
assist self-represented litigants in presenting their case properly so that the
process by which their disputes are resolved is fair and impartial. It is
imperative, however, that this duty be balanced with my duty to remain, at all
times, an impartial and neutral arbiter:
Rahman v. Windermere Valley
Property Management Ltd
.,
2022 BCCA 258
at para.
35
. As explained by
Justice Voith in
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2013 BCSC 1143
at para.
60
:

The courts will,
to the extent reasonably possible and depending on the history of a matter,
extend some indulgence to a self‑represented litigant who is not
conversant with the Rules or the law. Such indulgences do not, however, extend
to any diminution or impairment of another party's substantive rights.

[
15
]

Judges also must facilitate the proper administration of justice,
which includes the need to conserve scarce court resources. This is reflected
in the court’s inherent and residual jurisdiction to prevent an abuse of the
court’s process:
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79,
2003 SCC 63
at para.
35
.

[
16
]

Before me, Mr. Hong did his best to make focused submissions in
the application and, at all times, he was respectful in addressing the court. It
was evident that he spent considerable time preparing for the hearing and
reading numerous case authorities to educate himself as to the applicable law.
Nevertheless, I share Kirchner J.’s concern that his self-representation has
made this already complicated matter even more challenging for the court to
deal with. The joint records filed on the application were voluminous,
containing thousands of pages, in part because Mr. Hong insisted that
every affidavit he has sworn in these lengthy proceedings be included. As I
will discuss below, Mr. Hong’s lack of experience with the
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
has resulted in uncertainty and has increased the
procedural complexity of the proceedings.

[
17
]

I also have some concern that Mr. Hong has taken inconsistent
positions regarding the impact of his self-represented status. Before Kirchner
J., he argued strenuously that it was his right to self-represent and expressed
confidence in his ability to do so, arguing that he did not want to spend his
money on lawyers. Before me, Mr. Hong sought the Court’s indulgence on the
basis that because he was not a trained lawyer, and it took him considerably
longer to read and understand the case law. He also sought the Court’s
indulgence for not having turned his mind to how his claim could be amended in
light of the defendants’ position that his claims were inadequately pleaded; a
position he has been aware of since at least July 2025 when the defendants’
application materials were provided.

The Proceedings

[
18
]

As observed by Kirchner J., due to the steps taken by Mr. Hong,
there is now a confusing tangle of overlapping proceedings. Resolving these
applications requires an understanding of the extent to which the various proceedings
overlap or attempt to relitigate issues already determined. Accordingly, I
start with a high-level summary of each of the five proceedings commenced by
the plaintiffs.

Ontario Action

[
19
]

In June 2018, Mr. Hong and Beijing Hehe brought
a claim against Ka An, its managing director, Mr. Chang Yu Lui, the law
firm Fasken Martineau Dumoulin LLP (“Fasken”), and others in Ontario (the
“Ontario Action”). The Ontario Action alleged that Fasken had breached its
fiduciary duty by acting for both Beijing Hehe and Mr. Hong as well as Ka
An in the 2016 EPL share purchase. The allegations in that claim were
summarized by the Court of Appeal in
2538520 Ontario Limited v. Eastern
Platinum Limited
,
2020 BCCA 313
at para.
76
:

a)

[Mr. Hong] was in a
partnership with a company, Beijing Hehe Fengye Investment Co. Limited
(“Beijing Hehe”), to buy shares of EPL;

b)

in 2014, Beijing Hehe,
through its wholly owned company Hebei Zhongbo Platinum Co. Limited (“HZP”),
sought to purchase the Mine through a share purchase agreement for $225 million
because of the market value of its platinum and chrome reserves and other
metals, but in the end it decided not to proceed with that transaction;

c)

together, Mr. Hong
and Beijing Hehe determined it would be more profitable to buy a controlling
interest in EPL and take control of the EPL board. That would “combine the
resources of Beijing Hehe in selling metal reserves in China with [Mr. Hong’s]
networks of contacts and business experiences in Western business communities”;

d)

Mr. Hong and
Beijing Hehe’s primary advisor was a lawyer, Mr. Huang, of Fasken, who was
to negotiate with three larger EPL shareholders to purchase shares in EPL from
them;

e)

Fasken did not disclose
that at the same time it was acting for Ka An to the same ends, ultimately
assisting Ka An in purchasing shares in EPL in May and August 2016;

f)

Ka An’s
nominees were appointed to the Board of Directors of EPL in July 2016,
“frustrating” Beijing Hehe’s desire to control the Board;

g)

the defendant lawyers
misused confidential information including the existence of the opportunity to
buy EPL at significantly below market value;

h)

the alleged wrongs
allowed Ka An and its owner, Mr. Liu, to buy “control shares” and control
the board of EPL;

i)

this
caused Mr. Hong damage in that he lost the opportunity, with Beijing Hehe,
to gain control of EPL’s Board by purchasing EPL’s shares from a major
shareholder; and

j)

the value of this lost opportunity is at least $225 million.

[
20
]

The claims against Ka An and Mr. Liu were dismissed in 2020 on
jurisdictional grounds.

Petition to Commence a Derivative
Action

[
21
]

In November 2018, 253 Ont. Ltd. applied for leave to bring a
derivative action on EPL’s behalf against the company’s current and former
directors (the “2018 Derivative Petition”). At that time, 253 Ont. Ltd. held a
4.74% stake in EPL. Mr. Hong was not a named party in this proceeding, but
as the CEO of 253 Ont. Ltd., provided evidence to support the application for
leave.

[
22
]

The decision of N. Smith J. indexed as
2019 BCSC 1446
(the “Smith
Decision”) set outs the facts in detail. At a high level, the petition alleged that
EPL breached its fiduciary duty and was negligent for entering into a series of
transactions with Union Goal in 2018, aimed at recovering marketable products
from stored mining tailings at the Crocodile River Mine. 253 Ont. Ltd. alleged
that these transactions were improvident for EPL because the required
investment in equipment would exceed any profit to EPL and all of the benefits
of recovering products from the tailings would flow to Union Goal. It was
alleged that EPL failed to conduct sufficient due diligence before entering
into the transactions and that the proposed defendants breached their fiduciary
duties by preferring the interests of others over that of EPL.

[
23
]

Justice N. Smith concluded that the allegations that EPL completed
the Union Goal Transaction because it was motivated by something other than
EPL’s best interests were not sufficiently particularized to ground a breach of
fiduciary duty.  Justice N. Smith also considered Mr. Hong’s evidence that
Union Goal may be related to a significant shareholder of Ka An as well as certain
officers of EPL, including Diana Hu, CEO of EPL, and Andrea Zhang, the COO of
EPL. However, Mr. Hong provided no evidence of such a relationship.
Justice N. Smith concluded that it was not in EPL’s best interests to require its
directors to defend themselves against the fiduciary breach allegations based
on nothing more than speculation: Smith Decision at paras. 31–32.

[
24
]

With respect to 253 Ont. Ltd.’s negligence claim, N. Smith J. found the
claim was not bound to fail and that the “best interests” element of the test
for leave had been met. However, he found that 253 Ont. Ltd. could not
establish that the derivative proceeding was being brought in good faith. In
reliance on the test for good faith articulated in
DeCotiis v. Petromin
Resources Ltd.,
2017 BCSC 514
at para.
48
, N. Smith J. assessed
whether there were ulterior motives for bringing the action. He considered it
significant that Mr. Hong did not initially disclose that he and Beijing
Hehe had been foiled in their attempt to gain control of EPL as a result of the
election of Ka An’s slate of directors: Smith Decision at paras. 52–58. Justice
N. Smith also considered evidence that Mr. Hong had made his own proposal
to buy chrome produced from EPL tailings.

[
25
]

Based on this evidence, N. Smith J. concluded that Mr. Hong, as
CEO of 253 Ont. Ltd., had personal interests separate from the concerns he may
have had for the best interests of EPL, and that these personal interests were
a significant motive for the proposed derivative action. Justice N. Smith
concluded that the most likely inference to be drawn from the evidence was that
the “proposed action is an attempt to continue Mr. Hong’s unsuccessful
takeover bid by other means to obtain retribution for that bid’s failure”:
Smith Decision at paras. 57–58. Based on these findings, N. Smith J. held
that 253 Ont. Ltd. failed to satisfy the good faith element of the test for
leave.

[
26
]

This decision was upheld on appeal:
2538520 Ontario Ltd. v.
Eastern Platinum,
2020 BCCA 313
at para.
68
(the “Derivative Appeal
Decision”). In particular, the Court of Appeal found that N. Smith J. did not
err in inferring that Mr. Hong was personally motived in bringing the
derivative claim: Derivative Appeal Decision at para. 84. The Court of
Appeal also found that there was “little doubt that Mr. Hong concluded
without evidence that there is something nefarious about EPL’s deal with Union
Goal”: Derivative Appeal Decision at para. 85.

[
27
]

After Mr. Hong was denied leave, Mr. Hong issued a press
release on March 2, 2020, describing his failed attempt to bring a derivative
action and inviting other concerned EPL shareholders to consider commencing a
similar derivative action to advance relief from EPL in respect of the Union
Goal Transaction. Another shareholder, Xialong Ren, took up Mr. Hong’s
invitation and brought a derivative action based on largely the same
allegations.

[
28
]

Justice Gomery (as he then was) granted leave to Ms. Ren to
commence a revised derivative action only against the defendant Diana Hu. That
action remains ongoing. In that action, the court will be asked to resolve allegations
that Ms. Hu breached her fiduciary duty:

a)

by failing to disclose her relationship with Union Goal when she
caused EPL to enter into the Union Goal Transaction;

b)

by instructing others to manipulate information to reduce the value
of the transaction and preventing investigations into the true value of the Union
Goal Transaction; and

c)

by failing to cause EPL to take steps to enforce its rights under
the Union Goal Transaction despite Union Goal not having satisfied its
obligations under the agreements in breach of their fiduciary obligations.

[
29
]

Justice Gomery did not accept EPL’s argument that Ms. Ren’s
proceeding was an abuse of process, finding that there was “no evidence to
suggest that Ms. Ren had anything at all to do with any of the matters
that called into question Mr. Hong’s good faith”:
Ren v. Eastern
Platinum Limited,
2023 BCSC 404
at para.
48
. I will refer to this
proceeding as the “Ren Derivative Action”.

[
30
]

I now turn to describe the three proceedings before me in this
application.

Oppression Action – S201427

[
31
]

In February 2020, after the dismissal of the 2018 Derivative Petition,
and while the appeal of that decision was ongoing, Mr. Hong and 253 Ont.
Ltd. filed a claim against EPL and other defendants alleging oppression (the
“Oppression Action”). The notice of civil claim in the Oppression Action was
amended on June 11, 2021, to remove eight defendants after the claim was partly
struck by consent under R. 9-5.

[
32
]

The Oppression Action alleges that EPL acted oppressively by failing
to enforce the terms of a confidentiality agreement that it had with Horizon
International Development Ltd. (“Horizon”), an entity related to Ka An. It is
alleged that the failure to enforce this confidentiality agreement resulted in
Ka An acquiring the controlling stake of EPL in 2016. This conduct occurred
before 253 Ont. Ltd. became a shareholder in EPL.

[
33
]

In addition to the oppression allegations, the Oppression Action alleges
that eight defendants, including Ka An, committed the tort of conspiracy by
acting “in concert, by agreement and with a common design and intention to
acquire control of the EPL board.” It is further alleged that “in so doing,
Horizon breached the terms of the Confidentiality Agreement.” It is alleged
that this conduct was directed toward the plaintiffs including by unfairly
defeating Mr. Hong in the 2016 proxy battle.

[
34
]

The specific factual allegations underlying the oppression claim are
that while Mr. Hong was attempting to acquire shares in EPL, a state-owned
Chinese entity, China Arts (Far East) Ltd. (“China Arts”), was attempting to
acquire the same shares, in part, through Horizon. It is further alleged that
EPL agreed to give Horizon access to confidential information pursuant to a
confidentiality agreement in which Horizon agreed not to acquire a controlling
interest in EPL.

[
35
]

253 Ont. Ltd. and Mr. Hong allege that after the
confidentiality agreement was executed, the defendant Ms. Hu incorporated
Ka An and with the benefit of “the material information that was not publicly
disclosed, attempted and did ultimate acquire a controlling stake in EPL.” It
is alleged that EPL should have known that Ka An was effectively Horizon and
that it was a breach of the confidentiality agreement for Ka An to attempt to
acquire a controlling stake in EPL. It is further alleged that EPL failed to
take steps to enforce the confidentiality agreement.

[
36
]

The Oppression Action also pleads the law of negligence and breach
of fiduciary duty but does not include any material facts to describe the
duties owed or any breach of those duties under these causes of action.

[
37
]

253 Ont. Ltd. seeks orders requiring Ka An sell its shares in EPL, for
EPL to hold a new election of directors, and appoint a new CEO and COO. It also
seeks damages of US$50 million against six of the defendants.

[
38
]

The claim in this proceeding also originally contained allegations impugning
EPL’s transaction with Union Goal as being financially disastrous for EPL and
that the directors of EPL, including Ms. Hu, failed to conduct proper due
diligence prior to entering the transaction. The same allegations were made in the
2018 Derivative Petition that was dismissed by Justice N. Smith.

[
39
]

On June 17, 2021, all references to the Union Goal Transaction were
removed from the Oppression Action pursuant to the terms of a consent order
spoken to before Justice Branch. The order dismissed all claims against those defendants
against whom the Union Goal allegations were the sole allegations against them.
The order provides that the dismissal was made as if adjudged on their merits. This
took place after Ms. Hu and Andrea Zhang, who at that time were jointly
represented, filed an application to strike on the basis of abuse of process. Justice
Branch adjourned the application to strike generally.

Great Wall Action – S244818

[
40
]

On April 3, 2023, Mr. Hong wrote to EPL’s auditor, PWC, and
alleged that EPL engaged in related party transactions with Great Wall Enterprises
Inc. (“Great Wall”) pertaining to the sale of chrome concentrate at discounted
prices in 2022 (the “Great Wall Action”). In response, EPL’s board struck a
special committee to investigate. In December 2023, the special committee found
the allegations to be unsubstantiated.

Legal Framework

[
51
]

As these applications engage Rules 9-5 and 9-6
as well as abuse of process, I will first set out the overarching legal
principles I must apply to resolve them. These applications also raise legal
issues relating to oppression claims, derivative actions, and the scope of
recoverable economic loss. I will canvass the applicable law in my analysis of
each application.

Principles Applicable to Rule 9-6

[
52
]

Under R. 9-6, a responding party may, after serving a responding
pleading, “apply … for judgment dismissing all or part of a claim” if the court
is “satisfied that there is no genuine issue for trial”: Rule 9-6(4) and Rule
9-6(5)(a).

[
53
]

An application for summary judgment under R.
9-6 is not a trial by affidavit. Rather than trying the issues, the court is to
determine whether there are genuine issues to be tried. The key principles
applicable under R. 9-6 were summarized by the Court of Appeal in
Beach
Estate v. Beach,
2019 BCCA 277
(citations omitted):

[48] … Rule 9-6 is a challenge on a limited
review of evidence. A defendant can succeed on a Rule 9-6 application by
showing the case pleaded by the plaintiff is unsound or by adducing sworn
evidence that gives a complete answer to the plaintiff’s case … Such evidence
generally is adduced in the form of an affidavit.
If the court is satisfied
that the plaintiff is bound to lose or the claim has no chance of success, the
defendant must succeed on the Rule 9-6 application.
Conversely, if the
plaintiff submits evidence contradicting the defendant’s evidence in some
material respect or if the defendant’s evidence in support of the Rule 9-6
application fails to meet all of the causes of action raised by the plaintiff’s
pleadings, the application must be dismissed: …

[Emphasis
added.]

[
54
]

A summary judgment application “must be judged on the basis of the
pleadings and materials actually before the judge, not on suppositions about
what might be pleaded or proved in the future”:
Canada (Attorney General) v.
Lameman,
2008 SCC 14
at para.
19
. While evidence is admissible, a
judge is not permitted to weigh evidence on a R. 9-6 application beyond
determining whether the evidence is not disputed. Any further weighing should
be reserved for trial:
Beach Estate

at para.
49
.

[
55
]

The bar to be met by the defendants in this application is high. To
satisfy the court that there is no genuine issue for trial, the defendants must
show beyond a reasonable doubt that the plaintiffs are bound to lose:
Beach
Estate

at para.
65
. If an issue arises requiring the court to weigh
and assess evidence, then it cannot be said that it is plain and obvious or
beyond a doubt that the plaintiffs are bound to lose:
Beach

at para.
67
.

Principles Applicable to Rule 9-5

[
56
]

Under R. 9-5(1)(a) a pleading may be struck on
the basis that it discloses no reasonable claim. On a R 9-5 application, evidence
is not admissible, and the court does not weigh the evidence in its assessment.
Instead, the court must be satisfied that it is “plain and obvious, assuming
the material facts pleaded to be true, that, as a matter of law, the pleading
discloses no reasonable cause of action” or that “the claim has no reasonable
prospect of success”:
H.M.B. Holdings Limited v. Replay Resorts Inc.,
2021
BCCA 142
[
H.M.B. Holdings
] at para.
48
, citing
R. v. Imperial
Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC 42
at para.
17
; see also
Hunt
v. Carey Canada Inc.
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at 980,
1990 CanLII 90
. This
is a high threshold for the defendants to meet.

[
57
]

The fact that a claim is novel is not, in and of
itself, a sufficient basis to strike it as disclosing no reasonable cause of
action. However, where a novel claim is doomed to fail, it is in the interests
of the administration of justice that it be disposed of at an early stage, so
scarce judicial resources are not wasted on a lengthy and complex trial:
Atlantic
Lottery Corp. Inc. v. Babstock,
2020 SCC 19
.

[
58
]

While the material facts alleged must be assumed
to be true, it is well-established that the court need not accept as true
allegations that are incapable of proof or that consist of bald conclusory
statements or speculation. Such allegations do not qualify as material facts:
H.M.B.
Holdings

at para.
54
; see also
Kindylides v. Does,
2020 BCCA
330
at para.
35
. Where a pleading contains “vague, general references to
bad faith, discrimination, criminality, fraud and abuse”, the court must look
behind those allegations to determine whether they are grounded in real material
facts set out in the claim before taking them as true:
Samuda v. Knight,
2019
BCSC 133
at para.
23

[
59
]

The requirement to plead material facts is
central to the primary purpose of pleadings: to inform the defendant of the case
he or she must meet. This requirement is grounded in trial fairness. As Justice
Burke observed in
Samuda

at para.
20
, “the defendants at trial
should not have to guess what it is they are alleged to have done.”

[
60
]

At the same time, if the court finds the
material facts to be lacking but the pleading could be amended to disclose a reasonable
cause of action, the claim should not be struck without leave to amend:
Carhoun
& Sons Enterprises Ltd. v. Canada (Attorney General),
2015 BCCA 163
at para.
133
.
In
Beach Estate

at para.
68
, the Court of Appeal commented on the
application of this principle in claims brought by self‑represented
litigants, stating that, where a pleading is defective but does not meet the
“no triable issue” threshold, the proper course is to strike the pleading and
permit the litigant to seek appropriate amendments.

[
61
]

Accordingly, while the court must read pleadings
generously to account for  drafting deficiencies and consider whether defects
may be cured by amendment, it will only strike a claim with leave to amend
where it is satisfied that a viable amendment could elevate the claim beyond
the no-triable issue threshold: see
McNutt v. A.G. Canada et al.,
2004
BCSC 1113
at para.
27
.

[
62
]

Under R. 9-5(1)(b), a pleading that is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious may be struck. The test under
this subrule was helpfully summarized by Justice Fisher in
Willow v. Chong
,
2013
BCSC 1083
at para.
20
:

[20]      Under
Rule 9-5(1)(b), a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action, if it does not advance any claim known
in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it would
serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the court’s time and public
resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish
Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160
(S.C.);
Skender v Farley
,
2007 BCCA 629
. If a pleading is so
confusing that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, it may also be
unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious. An application under this sub-rule may be
supported by evidence.

[
63
]

The courts in this province have repeatedly
endorsed the following non-exhaustive list of considerations in determining
whether a proceeding is vexatious:
Gong v. O’Neill,
2022 BCSC 2119
at para.
68
,
aff’d
Gong v. Zhang
,
2023 BCCA 462
;
Simon v. Canada (Attorney
General)
,
2015 BCSC 924
at para.
97
, aff’d
Simon v.
British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
2016 BCCA 52
:

(a)

the bringing of one or more actions
to determine an issue which has already been determined by a court of competent
jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious proceeding;

(b)

where it is obvious that an action
cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no
reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief, the action is
vexatious;

(c)

vexatious actions include
those brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression
of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than
the assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)

it is a general characteristic of
vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised tend to be rolled forward
into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions
brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in
earlier proceedings;

(e)

in determining whether proceedings
are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the matter and not
just whether there was originally a good cause of action;

(f)

the failure of the person
instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings is one
factor to be considered in determining whether proceedings are vexatious; and

(g)

the
respondent’s conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial
decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal proceedings.

[
64
]

Under R. 9-5(1)(c), the basis upon which a
pleading can be struck as “embarrassing” is described by the Court of Appeal in

Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at para.
7
,
1985
CanLII 417 (C.A.)
:

…
[“embarrassing” means] that the allegations are so irrelevant that to allow them
to stand would involve useless expense, and would also prejudice the trial of
the action by involving the parties in a dispute that is wholly apart from the
issues. In order that allegations should be struck out from a defence upon that
ground… their irrelevancy must be quite clear and, so to speak, apparent at the
first glance. It is not enough that on considerable argument it may appear that
they do not afford a defence.

[
65
]

Under R. 9-5(1)(d), the court can strike a proceeding
where it is plain and obvious that it constitutes an abuse of process:
Daum
v. Gorrell,
2018 BCSC 225
at para.
37
.

[
66
]

Some of the relevant considerations on such an
application were summarized by Justice Forth in
Gong
as follows at para. 69:

… When
determining whether the proceedings constitute an abuse of process, the court
may consider whether its process is being used dishonestly or unfairly, or for
some ulterior or improper purpose, and whether there have been multiple or
successive related proceedings that are likely to cause vexation or oppression:…

[
67
]

While a proceeding that is vexatious may share
many factors in common with a proceeding that constitutes an abuse process, the
latter is a wider concept which encompasses any circumstance in which the
court’s process is used for an improper purpose. Abuse of process is a flexible
doctrine, and the categories of what may constitute an abuse of process are not
closed:
Freshway Specialty Foods v. Map Produce LLC
,
2005 BCSC 1485
at
para.
52
; see also
Daum

at para.
37
.

[
68
]

Judges have the inherent and residual discretion
to prevent an abuse of the court’s process:
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E.,
Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at para.
35
. Judges may also find a
proceeding to be an abuse of process where allowing it to proceed would be
contrary to the principles of judicial economy, consistency and finality:
Toronto
(City)
at para.
37
.

[
69
]

With respect to the multiplicity of proceedings, the abuse of
process doctrine can be utilized to prevent an abuse of the court’s process
through relitigation in a situation even where one or more of the requirements
of issue estoppel are not met:
Lamb v. Canada (Attorney General),
2017
BCSC 1802
at para.
81
.

[
70
]

To establish relitigation as an abuse of
process, it was held by Justice Smith in
Skender v. Farley
,
2007 BCCA
629
at para.
41
that the following pre-conditions must exist:

1.         The
parties are not the same in both actions;

2.         The
prior judicial decision is final;

3.

The second action seeks to relitigate an issue decided in the prior
action; and

4.
To relitigate the issue would have the effect of
impugning the authority and finality of the judgment in the prior action and
concerns would arise in the minds of reasonable observers about the integrity
of the justice system if the judgments should be inconsistent.

80
]

With respect to the claim for oppression, the grounds raised by the

The plaintiffs have no standing to bring an oppression claim;

b)

If the plaintiffs have standing, the claim is not timely as required

Business Corporation Act,
S.B.C. 2002, c. 57

[
BCA
]
;

c)

The claim is statute-barred under the
Limitation Act,
S.B.C.
2012, c. 13
;

d)

The claim is not grounded in a breach of reasonable expectations;

]

The plaintiffs have suffered no legal injury;

There was no unlawful act;

Who may bring an oppression claim?

[
82
]

As standing is a threshold issue, I will first address whether 253
Ont. Ltd. and Mr. Hong have standing to bring their oppression claim. The
defendants argue that the plaintiffs do not fall within the definition of
persons who are entitled to seek relief for oppressive conduct under
s. 227

of the
BCA
.

[
83
]

Section 227(2)
of the
BCA

states:

(2) A shareholder may apply to the court for
an order under this section on the ground

(a) that the
affairs of the company are being or have been conducted, or that the powers of
the directors are being or have been exercised, in a manner oppressive to one
or more of the shareholders, including he applicant, or

(b) that some act of the company has been
done or is threatened, or that some resolution of the shareholders or of the
shareholders holding shares of a class or series of shares has been passed or
is proposed, that is unfairly prejudicial to one or more of the shareholders,
including the applicant.

[
84
]

Section 227(1)
of the
BCA

defines
shareholder as:

For the purposes of this section,
"shareholder" has the same meaning as in section 1(1) and includes a
beneficial owner of a share of the company and any other person whom the court
considers to be an appropriate person to make an application under this
section.

[
85
]

Section 1(1)
of the
BCA

defines “shareholder” as “a person
whose name is entered in a securities register of a company as a registered
owner of a share of the company”.

[
86
]

As result, the scope of people who may seek an oppression remedy
under
s. 227(2)
is limited to shareholders, beneficial owners of company
shares, and persons the court considers to be an appropriate person to make the
application.

[
87
]

It is “well-established that a plaintiff may pursue an action for
oppression only in respect of wrongs suffered
qua
shareholder, and not
for wrongs suffered in other capacities:”
Yen v. Ghahramani
,
2023 BCCA
403
at para.
24
, citing
Dubois v. Milne
,

2020
BCCA 216
at

para.
113
. As a result, a person who is both a
shareholder and an employee may not bring an oppression claim for harms arising
from his or her employment:
Dubois

at

para.
113
. The
rationale behind this principle is that the cornerstone of the oppression
remedy is to protect a shareholder’s reasonable expectations:
BCE Inc. v.
1976 Debentureholders,
2008 SCC 69
at para.
68
.

[
88
]

In addition, to be entitled to relief under
s. 227
of the
BCA
,

253 Ont. Ltd. and Mr. Hong must demonstrate not only that the actions
of the directors of EPL fell short of their reasonable expectations, but that
they were directly and specifically harmed in a way that is separate from harm
suffered by the company more generally. If impugned actions are harmful to the
company as a whole, rather than to shareholders, that harm can only be remedied
through a derivative action under
s. 232
of the
BCA
:
Tassone v.
Smith,
2025 BCSC 163 (CanLII)
, 2025 BCSC163 at para.
67
, citing
Pasnak v. Chura,

2004 BCCA 221
at
paras.
5
, 27.

[
89
]

The defendants submit that to the extent that the oppression claim
seeks damages for the diminution of EPL’s share value, there is no basis to say
that this caused unique and direct harm to the plaintiffs separate from the
harm suffered by the company as a whole as a result of the loss of share value.

[
90
]

In assessing a claim for oppression, the court must conduct two
inquiries: 1) does the evidence support the reasonable expectation asserted by
the claimant? and if so, 2) does the evidence demonstrate that the reasonable
expectation was violated by conduct falling within the terms of “oppression”,
“unfair prejudice” or “unfair disregard” of a relevant interest?:
BCE Inc.

at
para.
68
.

[
91
]

The time for assessing a shareholder’s reasonable expectations is at
the time that they acquired shares. Oppression claims made by shareholders in
respect of allegedly oppressive conduct prior to their acquisition of shares have
been found to be unfounded:
Ford Motor Company of Canada Ltd. v. Ontario
Municipal Employees Retirement Board
, 79 O.R. (3d) 81,
2006 CanLII 15 (C.A.)
;

Hollinger Canadian Publishing Holdings Co. v. Mostad Publications Ltd.,
2007
BCSC 1496
at para.
47
.

(a)

92
]

94
]

]

(b)

Positions of the Parties

[
96
]

The defendants submit that because neither Mr. Hong nor 253

shareholder.

[
97
]

The defendants further submit that the plaintiffs do not fall within

s. 227(1)
of the
BCA
.

They rely on authorities in which the courts have concluded that the
following categories of persons do not qualify as appropriate persons under the
statute:

•

A director of the company that held a mere
option to purchase company shares:
Benarroch v. City Resources (Canada) Ltd.
,
54 B.C.L.R. (2d) 373,
1991 CanLII 896 (C.A.)
.

•

A company that had redeemed its shares in a
settlement agreement (and which sought to enforce that agreement through an
oppression claim):
Gierc Jr. v. Wescon Cedar Products Ltd.,
2021 BCSC 23

at para.
49
.

•

A director of a company who was denied by a
board resolution a transfer of company shares to which he believed he was
entitled:
Lee v. rnational Consort Industries Inc.
, 63 B.C.L.R. (2d) 119,

1992 CanLII 1076 (C.A.)
.

[
98
]

The decision in
N’Quatqua Logging Co. Ltd. v. Thevarge
,
2006
BCSC 1122
, is instructive. The Court explained, at para. 19, that the
concept of an “appropriate person” under the oppression remedy is intended to
extend protection to individuals who are not shareholders but who, because of
their relationship with or dealings with the corporation, have an interest
analogous to that of a shareholder. However, the Court made clear that this
category does not include individuals or entities that merely sought, but
failed, to acquire an ownership interest in the company.

[
99
]

In

Lee

at para.
17
,
the Court of Appeal made it
clear the category of appropriate persons cannot apply where “the oppressive
conduct … complain[ed] of is denial of [the person’s] status as a member.”

[
100
]

The defendants submit that this observation is analogous here. The
plaintiffs complain that Ka An won the share purchase and proxy battle
unfairly, and that EPL failed to stop them. This amounts to a claim that Mr. Hong
and Beijing Hehe should have gained control of EPL, not Ka An, and, as such, it
cannot be established that they suffered harm as shareholders.

[
101
]

For their part, the plaintiffs submit that the issue of standing
requires a final ruling on disputed facts and competing inferences. The basis
for this position is not clearly articulated, but it appears that the
plaintiffs wish to have the Court consider whether the alleged breach of the
confidentiality agreement harmed Mr. Hong, presumably in the proxy battle,
or influenced 253 Ont. Ltd. to become a shareholder of EPL in 2017.

[
102
]

The plaintiffs fail to address head-on the defendants’ position that
they do not have standing because at the time of the alleged harm, they were
neither shareholders, nor appropriate persons. The plaintiffs contend that
whether they are, in fact, appropriate persons is itself a triable issue but
offers no argument as to why they would be considered appropriate persons.

[
103
]

In response to the defendants’ argument that all the conduct
complained of pre-dates 253 Ont. Ltd.’s status as a shareholder, the plaintiffs
submit that they have standing because the oppressive conduct continued beyond
2016 and has affected 253 Ont. Ltd. after it became a shareholder in 2017.

[
104
]

The plaintiffs submit that, as a matter of law, pre-shareholding
conduct can form the basis for an oppression claim. In support of this
proposition, they rely on the decision of the Ontario Superior Court in
Ninth
Square Capital v. Boyes et al,
2021 ONSC 3878
[
Ninth Square
], for
the proposition that pre-shareholding conduct may be relevant where it is
concealed, forms part of continuing course of conduct or affects the
complainant after it becomes a shareholder. As I explain in the next section,
Ninth
Square
does not stand for this proposition and provides no assistance to
the plaintiffs.

(c)

Analysis: The Plaintiffs Do Not Have Standing

[
105
]

Based on a review of the pleadings, including the plaintiffs’
admissions, there is no dispute that the plaintiffs’ alleged reasonable
expectations relate to events that pre-date 253 Ont. Ltd.’s acquisition of
shares. Therefore, the plaintiffs do not have standing as shareholders to bring
an oppression claim.

[
106
]

Ninth Square
does not support the
plaintiffs’ argument that the pre-shareholding conduct can form the basis of an
oppression claim. In
Ninth Square
,
there was no pre-shareholding conduct
at issue because there was no dispute that Ninth Square was a beneficial
shareholder having entered into a valid and enforceable contract to receive
shares in a publicly traded company, MPX. Ninth Square was a 50% shareholder in
Spartan, a private cannabis company, and had agreed to sell it shares in
Spartan to MPX in return for shares in MPX. At the same time, and unknown to
Ninth Square, MPX was negotiating to sell itself to iAnthus Capital Holdings.
That sale was structured such that MPX amalgamated with a wholly owned
subsidiary of iAnthus and its assets were transferred to a new private
corporation, MPXI. As part of the sale, MPX assigned the share purchase
agreement with Ninth Square to iAnthus. Ninth Square did not consent to this
assignment. However, when Ninth Square learned of the assignment, it was
promised shares in iAnthus. Instead, it received only shares in MPXI. Ninth
Square’s core allegation was that it was oppressed because it had contracted to
sell its Spartan shares in exchange for shares in a publicly traded company but,
instead, received shares in a privately traded company.

[
107
]

The defendants in
Ninth Square

argued that an oppression
remedy was not available because the conduct complained of arose before Ninth
Square

actually became a shareholder of any MPX entity. The Court
rejected this argument finding that the oppression claim was not based on Ninth
Square’s

reasonable expectation of becoming a shareholder but on a
written contract. On this basis, the Court found that there was no dispute that
Ninth Square was a beneficial shareholder entitled to receive shares. The same
cannot be said in the case before me. At no time did the plaintiffs assume the
status of shareholder or beneficial shareholder prior to the alleged oppressive
conduct.

[
108
]

In any event
,
the plaintiffs’ submission that the defendants
engaged in continuing oppressive conduct beyond 2016 that effected 253 Ont.
Ltd. after it became a shareholder in 2017, is not grounded in either the amended
notice of civil claim for the Oppression Action or the plaintiffs’ response to
a demand for particulars. The pleadings regarding oppression focus on alleged
acts leading up to the July 5, 2016 proxy battle which caused Mr. Hong to
lose the opportunity to acquire control of EPL. How that conduct continued past
September 2017 is not set out in the pleadings. While in respect of the
conspiracy claim, the particulars refer to ongoing conduct by the alleged
conspirators and EPL commencing before the proxy battle and ongoing to 2021 to
strip the value out of EPL, suppress its share value, and increase EPL’s
liabilities. Even if these allegations were pleaded in support of the
oppression claim, they do not amount to the direct and specific harm required
to constitute oppressive conduct. Claims based on actions that reduce the share
price and undermine the financial health of the company as a whole are properly
the subject of a derivative action under
s. 232
of the
BCA
:
Tassone

at
para.
67
.

[
109
]

I am also satisfied that the issue of whether the plaintiffs are
appropriate persons to bring an oppression claim is not a genuine issue for
trial. Having been put on notice of the defendants’ position, the plaintiffs
were required to respond substantively to explain their status as appropriate
persons and have failed to do so. As an unsuccessful bidder for control of a
publicly traded company, Mr. Hong does not fall within the small class of
appropriate persons with a
direct
financial interest in the financial
management of EPL. 253 Ont. Ltd. was not in existence at the time of the
alleged oppressive conduct and, therefore, cannot be said to have had a direct
financial interest in EPL immediately prior to the oppressive conduct.

[
110
]

Accordingly, I am satisfied that the oppression claim raises no
genuine issue for trial and that it should be struck under R. 9-6. Given this
conclusion, it is not necessary for me to consider the defendants’ argument
that the oppression claim has not been brought in a timely manner. Although Mr. Hong
sought leave during oral submissions to make amendments to his pleadings, the
lack of standing is a defect that cannot be cured through an amendment. The law
is equally clear that Mr. Hong’s desire to take over EPL does not give him
standing to advance an oppression proceeding.

Required Elements for Tort of
Unlawful Act Conspiracy

[
111
]

I now turn to my assessment of the plaintiffs’
conspiracy claim. The elements of the tort of unlawful act conspiracy are:

a.

the defendants acted in combination by agreement or common design;

b.

the defendants committed an unlawful act;

c.

the defendants’ conduct was directed towards the plaintiffs;

d.

the defendants knew or ought to have known that injury to the
plaintiffs was likely to result from their unlawful act; and

e.

the defendants’ unlawful conduct in furtherance of their conspiracy
caused injury to the plaintiffs.

(
LeRoy v. Timberwest Forest
Corp.
,

2021 BCCA 326
at para.
80
.)

(a)

Review of the Conspiracy Pleadings

[
112
]

In the Oppression Action, the plaintiffs allege
in the amended notice of civil claim that at the time Mr. Hong was
attempting to gain control of EPL, Ms. Hu and Andrea Zhang (who later
became officers of EPL) had roles with Horizon. It is alleged that Horizon was
being used by a state-owned Chinese company, China Arts, to acquire the same
shares of EPL that Mr. Hong wished to acquire. In connection with
Horizon’s due diligence, EPL is alleged to have given Horizon access to confidential
information and required Horizon to execute a confidentiality agreement in
which Horizon agreed that it would not acquire a controlling interest in EPL or
attempt to take over the EPL board.

[
113
]

It is alleged that Ms. Hu then incorporated
Ka An in June 2015 to get around the confidentiality agreement between Horizon
and EPL, and that Ka An went on to acquire a controlling stake in EPL. It is
alleged that EPL should have known that Ka An was effectively Horizon and that EPL
failed to take any steps to enforce the confidentiality agreement.

[
114
]

The alleged conspiracy is set out in the
following paragraphs:

[33] Mr. Sun, Mr. Liu, Ms. Hu,
Mr. Zhang, Horizon, Ka An, China Taurus and China Arts acted in concert,
by agreement and with a common design and intention to acquire control of the
EPL board. In so doing, Horizon breached the terms of the Confidentiality
Agreement. That conduct was directed toward the plaintiff, including by
unfairly defeating Mr. Hong in the 2016 proxy battle.

[34] This caused
damage to the plaintiffs for which Horizon, Ka An, China Taurus, China Arts, Ms. Hu,
Mr. Zhang, Mr. Sun and Mr. Liu are liable.

[
115
]

The particulars set out further detail as to how this conspiracy is
alleged to have been carried out. The defendants raise the concern the
plaintiffs have not applied to amend their claim and submit that the plaintiffs
should not be permitted to expand their claim through particulars, the proper
function of which is to limit the generality of the pleadings:
Hayes
Heli-Log Services Ltd. v. Acro Aerospace Inc.,
2006 BCSC 80
at para.
5
.
Leaving aside the issue of whether the particulars improperly expand the
plaintiffs’ conspiracy claim, for present purposes it is sufficient to note
that the particulars align with the amended notice of civil claim in identifying
the breach of the confidentiality agreement as the alleged unlawful act
necessary to make out the conspiracy claim.

[
116
]

In the particulars, the plaintiffs allege that the conspirators used
the information covered by the confidentiality agreement to determine whether
EPL was a target worth acquiring. EPL is alleged to have become a
co-conspirator by terminating the confidentiality agreement to conceal the
defendants’ actions and further by seeking to conceal the defendants’ breach of
the agreement by terminating the confidentiality agreement.

(b)

Positions of the Parties

[
117
]

Ka An submits that the conspiracy allegations against it and Mr. Chang
Yu Liu amount to bald speculation devoid of the required material facts and
accordingly, warrant summary dismissal under R. 9-6. They focus on three key
failings in the pleadings:

a)

There is no pleading, nor any evidence, that Ka An and Mr. Liu
(the sole director of Ka An until April 2016) were parties to the
confidentiality agreement;

b)

The plaintiffs have failed to show that Mr. Liu, as an
individual, committed a tortious act that demonstrates an identity or interest
separate from that of the corporate defendant, Ka An:
Dorus v. Teck Corp.,
2001
BCSC 1201
at paras.
19–20
; and

c)

There are no material facts pleaded to demonstrate that the
defendants participated in the alleged unlawful conduct with the common intent
to injure the plaintiffs. Rather, the pleadings state only that the defendants wished
to obtain control of the EPL Board.

[
118
]

Further, Ka An submits that the plaintiffs have misrepresented the
terms of the confidentiality agreement and that on its face, it cannot support
the plaintiffs’ allegation that Ka An, Horizon, and EPL engaged in unlawful
conduct. Accordingly, it submits that there is no genuine issue for trial.

[
119
]

Ka An also submits that the conspiracy allegations are time-barred
having been brought outside the applicable limitation period.

[
120
]

EPL submits that the plaintiffs’ conspiracy must fail because the
unlawful act element cannot be met as the plaintiffs were not privy to the
confidentiality agreement and are, therefore, impermissibly seeking damages for
the breach of another person’s contract. They further submit that there is no
pleading or factual basis to support that either plaintiff was a third-party
beneficiary of the confidentiality agreement allegedly breached by Horizon.

[
121
]

EPL submits that claims based on breach of contract are distinct
from other legal claims because they are
in personam
in nature because
they are enforceable only against the parties to the contract:
Design
Services Ltd. v. Canada,
2008 SCC 22
[
Design Services
] at para.
39
.
They also

rely on the decision of Madam Justice Sharma in
Latifi v. The
TDL Group Corp.,
2021 BCSC 2183
, aff’d
2025 BCCA 45
. In
Latifi,
the
defendant sought to strike a notice of civil claim in a proposed class action,
including a claim for unlawful means conspiracy. The defendant, TDL, owned the
Tim Horton’s brand in Canada and was the franchisor for its Canadian locations.
The proposed representative plaintiff was a Tim Horton’s restaurant employee.
The claim took issue with a standard clause in the Tim Horton’s franchise
agreements with TDL that franchisees agreed not to hire any person employed by
TDL or any other franchisee. Among other things, the plaintiff alleged that TDL,
in insisting on and enforcing the no-hire clause, committed unlawful means
conspiracy and that the clause amounted to a restraint on trade.

[
122
]

TDL submitted that this claim was misconceived because the no-hire
clause did not exist in any contract with Tim Horton’s employees. Madam Justice
Sharma accepted the defendant’s submission and concluded that the conspiracy
claim based on unlawful means was bound to fail due to the lack of privity
between the plaintiff and the impugned contractual clause.

[
123
]

EPL also points to the Court of Appeal’s decision in
XY, LLC v.
Zhu,
2013 BCCA 352
at para.
50
, as an example of where an unlawful act
conspiracy claim succeeded against a third-party but only because the plaintiff
was privy to the particular contract that was allegedly breached.

[
124
]

The plaintiffs submit that the conspiracy claim raises genuine
factual issues and that the defendants have not met their burden of negating
such issues beyond a reasonable doubt:
Metro-Can Construction (HS) Ltd. v.
Noel Developments Ltd.
, 26 B.C.L.R. (3d) 26,
1996 CanLII 3329 (C.A.)
. The
plaintiffs further submit that issues of law can only be decided under R. 9-6
if there are no real disputes about the material facts and the applicable law
is well-settled by authoritative jurisprudence:
Wang v. Niu,
2022 BCSC
1027
at para.
20
. The plaintiffs argue that there are too many evidentiary
gaps and insufficient discovery to make the necessary findings to dismiss the
conspiracy claim.

(c)

Analysis: Do the Conspiracy Pleadings Raise a
Genuine Issue for Trial?

[
125
]

An allegation that parties have engaged in the
intentional tort of conspiracy is a serious one that calls on a plaintiff to
plead his or her case with heightened precision and clarity:
Gong
at para. 66.
The standards for pleading a conspiracy are long-standing and well-known
.
In

H.M.B. Holdings

at para.
67
, the British Columbia Court of Appeal
endorsed the following passage from Bullen, Leake & Jacob's
Precedents
of Pleadings
, 13th ed. (1990):

The statement of
claim should describe who the several parties to the conspiracy are and their relationship
with each other. It should allege the conspiracy between the defendants giving
the best particulars it can of the dates when or dates between which the
unlawful conspiracy was entered into or continued, and the intent to injure ...
It should state precisely the objects and means of the alleged conspiracy to
injure and the overt acts which are alleged to have been done by each of the
alleged conspirators in pursuance of the conspiracy, and lastly, the injury and
damage occasioned to the plaintiff ...

[
126
]

The conspiracy pleadings in this case fall well short of this
standard in respect of the requirement to plead material facts to support the necessary
element that the defendant’s conduct must be directed towards the plaintiff. The
allegation going to this element in both the notice of civil claim and
particulars amount to one bald conclusory statement that the conduct was
directed towards Mr. Hong to unfairly defeat him in the proxy battle.
While the particulars allege that Mr. Liu was advised, at some unspecified
time, that Mr. Hong was a competitor seeking control of EPL, there is no
allegation that Mr. Liu undertook the alleged conspiracy to specifically
target Mr. Hong. Further, there is no allegation pleaded that Mr. Liu
committed the conspiracy to advance his personal interests separate from that
of Ka An: see
Dorus

at paras.
19–20
.

[
127
]

While the pleadings are replete with speculation that Mr. Hong
lost the proxy battle because the confidentiality agreement was breached which allowed
his competitors to gain an unfair advantage, there is very little in the way of
material facts to support this conclusory pleading. The pleadings fail to
identify conduct on the part of the defendants outside the realm of legitimate
competitive activity in the acquisition of shares in a public company.

[
128
]

More fundamentally, I am persuaded that there is no genuine issue
that the alleged breach of the confidentiality agreement constitutes unlawful
conduct for the purposes of conspiracy. The agreement was entered into on
January 6, 2016, between Horizon and EPL. Ka An is not a party to the
agreement. Contrary to Mr. Hong’s characterization, the agreement does not
prohibit Horizon (or as Mr. Hong alleges, Horizon acting as Ka An) from
acquiring shares in EPL. The agreement specifically carves out the ability of
Horizon to acquire EPL shares either from a number of specifically named
corporate entities and its affiliates or otherwise from another source with the
written consent of EPL. Two of the named entities are Invesco Canada Ltd. (“Invesco”)
and Harrington Global Ltd. (“Harrington”). Even if one assumes the truth of the
allegation that Horizon was Ka An, the confidentiality agreement itself did not
amount to an outright prohibition on the acquisition of EPL shares.

[
129
]

In its response to civil claim, Ka An denies that it was a party to
the confidentiality agreement. In any event, it pleads that it acquired shares
in EPL in May 2016 from Invesco and in August 2016 from Harrington.

[
130
]

The lack of specificity in the pleadings, together with the fact
that the confidentiality agreement does not amount to a prohibition on the acquisition
of shares in EPL, cause me to conclude that the conspiracy claim raises no
genuine issue for trial and is struck as against all defendants.

[
131
]

As a result, there is no need for me to consider in detail whether
the conspiracy claim should also be struck as being beyond the limitation
period. Had this been the only basis raised by the defendants to strike the
claim, I would have concluded that Mr. Hong’s discoverability of the
agreement was an issue that should be resolved at trial.

[
132
]

I turn now to EPL’s submission that the plaintiffs’ lack of privity
to the confidentiality agreement is a fatal flaw such that the unlawful act
element of conspiracy is not met.

[
133
]

Having considered the case law relied upon by the defendants, I am
not satisfied the law surrounding the requirement of privity for unlawful means
conspiracy on the basis of a breach of contract is sufficiently settled to allow
me to conclude that beyond a reasonable doubt the claim is bound to fail on
this basis.

[
134
]

In
Latifi,
the plaintiff’s argument that
the no-hire clause constituted a restraint on trade was central to Sharma J.’s
reasoning. In this regard, she adopted the following submission as a sound
statement of law:

71. In other words, the purpose of the
contractual doctrine is to protect a contracting party’s ability to carry
out
its
work to carry on
its
trade, to carry
out
its
business; the doctrine is about a party voluntarily
contracting to restrict
its own
business activities to
its

own
detriment.
The doctrine is
not
about a contractual restraint that impacts
a stranger to the contract to the stranger’s detriment.

[Emphasis in
original.]

[
135
]

The case before me does not engage the doctrine of restraint of
trade. Rather, it concerns an alleged breach of a confidentiality agreement
that allegedly is said to have given Mr. Hong’s competitors an unfair
advantage. In my view, these facts do not implicate the policy concerns
underlying restraint of trade, which typically arise where a party voluntarily
agrees by contract to restrict its own activities. Here, the allegation is that
the breach of the agreement conferred an unfair advantage on the alleged
conspirators in the proxy contest. The issue is whether that breach constitutes
unlawful conduct for the purposes of the tort of conspiracy.

[
136
]

The reasoning of Court of Appeal in
XY, LLC

suggests that
there remains some uncertainty in the law regarding the scope of “unlawful
means” in the context of civil conspiracy. The Court of Appeal observed that
quasi-criminal conduct that is not itself actionable in tort is sufficient to
constitute unlawful conduct for the purposes of the conspiracy tort. It also
cited with approval the discussions in
Bank of Montreal v
.
Tortora,
2010
BCCA 139
; and
Agribands Purina Canada Inc. v. Kasamekas,
2011 ONCA 460
;
in the latter where the Ontario Court

notes that, at least in Australia,
the categories of unlawful means are not closed. Accordingly
,
I do not
read
Latifi
together with
XY, LLC
as definitively foreclosing a
claim in unlawful means conspiracy on the basis of breach of an agreement in
all circumstances where there is no privity. In my view, it remains possible
that the breach of a third-party agreement could, in some circumstances,
constitute unlawful conduct for the purposes of conspiracy, and it is not
appropriate to strike the conspiracy claim on this basis.

Is the alleged damage pure
economic loss that is not recoverable?

[
137
]

Having already struck the conspiracy claim as raising no genuine
issue, it is not strictly necessary for me to consider EPL’s submission that
the legal injury claimed by the plaintiffs is pure economic loss and that this
loss does not fit within the narrow categories of recoverable economic loss
recognized in the jurisprudence. Nonetheless, I will do so in the event that my
conclusions above are incorrect.

[
138
]

While I accept that the loss alleged by the plaintiffs, namely the
loss of opportunity to control the board of EPL, meets the definition of pure
economic loss, it appears from the pleadings that this loss is alleged to have
arisen as a result of the conspiracy, which is an intentional tort. There is
only passing reference to negligence in the pleadings and no material facts
supporting a duty of care or breach of that duty are included. As I read the
pleadings, the loss is alleged to have arisen as a result of the conspiracy.

(a)

Review of the Plaintiffs’ Pleadings that it
Suffered Loss

[
139
]

The plaintiffs allege that the conspiracy to
have Horizon breach the confidentiality agreement to unfairly defeat Mr. Hong
in the proxy battle caused them damage. The plaintiffs further particularized,
and reiterated in oral submissions, their loss consisted of the deprivation of
the opportunity to acquire a controlling interest in EPL due to the defendants’
unlawful use of the confidential information to gain a negotiating advantage. They
allege that, but for this misuse, Mr. Hong would have obtained control of
EPL and that he consequently suffered financial losses.

[
140
]

In the particulars, the plaintiffs provide further particulars that
the conspirators engaged in a campaign to strip the value out of EPL to
suppress its share price to allow Ka An and Horizon to solicit EPL’s shares at
a fraction of their trading price prior to the alleged conspirators taking control
of EPL in 2016. There is no allegation that these actions were specifically
directed at the plaintiffs. Mr. Hong conceded the loss to 253 Ont. Ltd.
arose after it became a shareholder in EPL and arises from the diminution of
the value of its shares.

(b)

Positions of the Parties

[
141
]

The EPL submits that the plaintiffs’ losses
associated with the loss of the proxy battle are untethered from any physical,
mental, or property damage and, therefore, do not constitute a legal injury for
the purposes of tort law. As such, they are pure economic losses as defined by
the Supreme Court of Canada in
1688782 Ontario Inc. v. Maple Leaf Foods Inc.,

2020 SCC 35
[
Maple Leaf Foods
] at para.
17
.

[
142
]

EPL relies on the following passage from
Maple
Leaf Foods
at para.
19
:

… While this Court has recognized that pure
economic loss may be recoverable in certain circumstances, there is no general
right,
in tort, protecting against the negligent or intentional infliction
of pure economic loss.
For example, economic loss caused by ordinary
marketplace competition is not, without something more, actionable in
negligence (
A.I. Enterprises Ltd. v. Bram Enterprises Ltd.
,
2014
SCC 12
, [2014] 1 S.C.R. 177, at para.
31
, citing
Mogul Steamship
Company v. McGregor
,
Gow & Co.

(1889), 23 Q.B.D. 598
(C.A.), at p. 614,
aff’d
[1892] A.C. 25 (H.L.)
). Such loss falls
outside the scope of a plaintiff’s legal rights — the loss is
damnum
absque injuria
and unrecoverable (E. J. Weinrib, “The
Disintegration of Duty” (2006), 31
Adv. Q.
212, at
p. 226; D. Nolan, “Rights, Damage and Loss” (2017), 37
Oxf. J.
Leg. Stud.
255, at pp. 262‑68). Indeed, the essential goal
of competition is to attract more business, which may mean taking business away
from others. Absent a contractual or statutory entitlement,
there is no
right to a customer or to the quality of a bargain, let alone to a market
share.
As Taylor J.A. wrote for the British Columbia Court of Appeal
in
Kripps v. Touche Ross & Co.
(1992),
1992 CanLII
923 (BC CA)
, 94 D.L.R. (4th) 284, at p. 297: …

[Emphasis added.]

[
143
]

The Supreme Court of Canada in
Maple Leaf Foods

sets out that
to recover any type of negligently caused loss, the plaintiff must prove all
the elements of the tort of negligence, namely: (1) the defendant owes the
plaintiff a duty of care; (2) the defendant’s conduct breached the standard of
care; (3) the plaintiff sustained damage; and (4) the defendant’s breach caused
the damage. The defendants submit that the plaintiffs’ alleged loss of
opportunity to gain control of EPL is purely economic and does not fall within
the three recognized categories of potentially recoverable economic loss set
out in
Maple Leaf Foods
,
namely:

a)

negligent misrepresentation or performance of a service;

b)

negligent supply of shoddy goods or structures; and

c)

relational economical loss.

[
144
]

The defendants submit that the first two categories are not engaged
and that the third is inapplicable. They submit that the third category applies
only where the defendant negligently causes personal injury or property damage
to a third party with whom the plaintiff has a relationship and the plaintiff
consequently suffers pure economic loss arising from that relationship:
Design
Services

at para.
33
.

[
145
]

The defendants submit that the pleadings do not allege a novel
category for the recovery of pure economic losses. Even if the pleadings had
done so, the defendants submit that the Supreme Court of Canada has expressed a
clear reluctance to extend the protection of tort law to economic losses arising
from failed commercial negotiations:
Martel Building Ltd. v. Canada,
2000
SCC 60
at paras.
67–72
. In light of this reluctance, they argue there is
no realistic prospect that the courts would recognize a new category of pure economic
loss to provide damages for Mr. Hong’s failed attempt to purchase shares
in a publicly traded company.

[
146
]

Although EPL squarely raised this argument in its notice of
application, the only submissions the plaintiffs advanced in response was to
argue that the decision in
Design Services

is distinguishable because,
in contrast to that case, the plaintiffs suffered an injury and it would be
premature to decide this injury is not recoverable in the absence of full
disclosure and discovery. In my view, discovery is not required for the Court
to consider, as a matter of law, whether the losses alleged are unrecoverable
pure economic losses.

[
147
]

Putting aside the failure of the pleadings to articulate the legal
basis for a novel duty of care in these circumstances, I recognize that
advancing such a legal argument is no easy task for Mr. Hong who is
self-represented as it requires the plaintiffs explain, as a matter of law,
what rights are at stake and whether a new category of economic loss should be
recognized. These facts require an analysis of whether the plaintiffs and the
defendants were in a sufficiently proximate relationship such that the
plaintiffs’ loss can be the subject of recovery in tort law: see
Maple Leaf
Foods

at paras.
22–23
.

[
148
]

Nevertheless, given the unique procedural history of this case and
the fact that Mr. Hong has had the defendants’ application materials since
July 2025, I am not satisfied that the plaintiffs’ lack of engagement in this
legal analysis is an obstacle to determining the pure economic loss argument on
its merits. I am mindful of Kirchner J.’s observations in the Kirchner Decision
that retaining counsel, at least to sort out issues with the pleadings in these
complicated and overlapping proceedings, would be of great benefit to Mr. Hong.
Despite this suggestion, Mr. Hong has chosen, for “good or bad”, in the
words of Kirchner J., to continue to represent himself. Mr. Hong did not
suggest before me that he was financially unable to retain counsel, only that
it is expensive to do so and he did not wish to incur that expense. Having been
put on notice of EPL’s position that the claimed loss is non-compensable pure
economic loss, he was obligated to engage with all aspects of that argument.

(c)

Analysis: The Plaintiffs’ Losses are
Non-Compensable

[
149
]

Having considered the pleadings and the jurisprudence drawn to my
attention by counsel, I am satisfied that the loss alleged by the plaintiffs,
namely the loss of opportunity to control the board of EPL, meets the
definition of pure economic loss. Mr. Hong did not have the right to
acquire a controlling interest. Further, the pleadings do not contain
sufficient material facts to ground any allegation that he lost the opportunity
to acquire EPL shares due to anything other than the operation of market forces
and competition.

[
150
]

As noted above there is no general right in tort which protects
against the negligent or intentional infliction of pure economic loss. As the
Supreme Court in
A.I. Enterprises v. Bram Enterprises Ltd,
2014 SCC 12

at para.
31
states, “the common law in general, and tort law in
particular, have been astute to assure “some elbow-room [many would say much
elbow-room] for the aggressive pursuit of self-interest”.

[
151
]

Accordingly, the common law has limited the recovery of pure
economic losses to strict categories. As the Supreme Court of Canada notes,
these categories “provide greater structure to a diverse range of factual
situations … that raise similar … concerns”: see
Maple Leaf Foods
at para.
22
.
The controlling concept remains proximity between the plaintiff and the
tortfeasor, not how the loss factually occurred.

[
152
]

I accept the defendants’ submission that the plaintiffs’ claim for
loss does not fall within one of the currently recognized categories of pure
economic loss. Nor do the plaintiffs address in their submissions on what
policy grounds a new category should be recognized to allow them to be
compensated for their loss of their opportunity to control EPL.

[
153
]

For the reasons set out above, the conspiracy allegations raise no
genuine issue for trial, and they should be struck under R. 9-6. For the same
reasons, the conspiracy allegations are bound to fail and, therefore, raise no reasonable
cause of action and can also be struck under R. 9-5(1)(a). Accordingly, the
conspiracy claim is struck.

b)

c)

of the
BCA
requires 253 Ont. Ltd. to seek leave of the court
by way of a petition to advance the oppression claim; and

d)

]

repetitive of any prior proceeding and that the causes of action it raises are
