s. 227
of the
BCA
.”

Analysis: The Great Wall Action is
a Derivative Claim

[
188
]

I will first address whether allegations are sufficient to disclose
a cause of action for shareholder oppression.

[
189
]

Section 227
of the
BCA

requires that a shareholder seeking an
oppression remedy to show “particular prejudice or damage beyond the diminution
in value of his or her shares as a result of allegedly oppressive conduct”:
1043325
Ontario Ltd. v. CSA Building Sciences Western Ltd
.,
2016 BCCA 258
at para.
78
.
If a shareholder fails to establish that it has suffered direct and special
harm as a result of the alleged oppressive conduct, leave to bring a derivative
action must be sought as per
s. 232
of the
BCA
:
Pasnak

at para.
5
.

[
190
]

Mr. Hong should be well aware from his experience with the 2018
Derivative Petition that, as a pre-requisite to being granted leave to commence
a derivative action, a shareholder must demonstrate that the proceeding is
being brought in good faith: Smith Decision at para.
27
. The defendants
contend that the plaintiff has deliberately framed this proceeding as an
oppression claim to overcome the leave requirement which, given N. Smith J.’s
findings that Mr. Hong was motivated by retribution for his unsuccessful
takeover bid, he is unlikely to satisfy.

[
191
]

There is some merit to this suggestion. During oral submissions, Mr. Hong
explained to the Court that he brought the Great Wall Action because it would
be less costly for him than a derivative action. Further, as part of what he
characterized as his “litigation strategy”, he could represent himself in an
oppression proceeding and would have “the freedom to make [his] own decisions
[about] what to do in the litigation”. He acknowledged that in a derivative
claim, because other shareholders would not be comfortable with him prosecuting
the claim on behalf of EPL, counsel would have to be retained at considerable
expense. Mr. Hong advised that he was not prepared to incur this
additional expense given legal fees he has incurred to date. Mr. Hong also
acknowledged given N. Smith J.’s finding that he lacked in good faith in the
2018 Derivative Petition, it would be an “uphill battle” to bring another
derivative action. However, he noted that the Smith Decision rested on a record
that did not include the more recent developments alleged in the Great Wall
Action.

[
192
]

Despite this admission, in his submissions, Mr. Hong contends
that 253 Ont. Ltd. has suffered unique and direct harms that are distinct from
any generalized harm to EPL. The following three unique and direct effects are
alleged:

a)

the diversion of corporate opportunities to Ka An and Mr. Liu
to the exclusion of other shareholders;

b)

The impairment of the plaintiff’s governance and voting interests
through the entrenchment of control by Ka An and its affiliates; and

c)

Informational oppression arising from the failure to disclose
material related-party transactions and conflicts of interest, thereby
depriving the plaintiff of the ability to protect its interests as a
shareholder.

[
193
]

These submissions do not entirely track the unique and direct
effects that are alleged in paras. 63–80 of the amended notice of civil claim.
For example, although not highlighted by Mr. Hong in his oral submissions,
the pleadings allege that the unlawful scheme by the defendants in respect of
the Great Wall transaction resulted in a significant loss of share value.

[
194
]

Having reviewed the pleadings, I am not persuaded that the claim
alleges any harms that would have been suffered uniquely and directly by 253
Ont. Ltd. As a publicly traded company, the loss of share value is a loss
suffered by the company and shareholders as a whole. The fact that Ka An
allegedly gained a larger share of EPL shares also does not have unique impacts
to the plaintiff. Likewise, the alleged failure to disclose information is
something that would impact all shareholders. The allegations do not show how
this conduct harmed the plaintiff in a unique way other than in its status as a
shareholder.

[
195
]

With respect to the diversion of corporate opportunities, a claim on
this basis is generally regarded as derivative. However, where the
opportunities are diverted to a majority shareholder, then the wrong impacts
the minority in a disparate manner and the claim assumes a personal character:
Gopal
v. Burke,
2007 BCSC 1930
at para.
15
. However, there is no allegation
that Ka An was a majority shareholder at the time of the Great Wall
transaction. Rather, it is alleged that Ka An, together with an entity called
Million Metro Investment and Regency Inc. Limited, own over 70% of the EPL
shares without any material facts to support the alleged connection between
these entities. In my view, this is a bald allegation that I am not obligated
to take as true in considering whether a reasonable cause of action for
oppression has been made out.

[
196
]

Accordingly, the Great Wall Action does not disclose a reasonable
cause of action for oppression and should be struck:
Bruneau v. Irwin
Industries (1978) Ltd.,
2002 BCSC 757
at para.
19
. All the harms
alleged are derivative, and leave is required for 253 Ont. Ltd. to advance any
claim in respect of the harms alleged. The Great Wall Petition suffers from the
same defect.

Analysis: The
Great Wall Proceedings Fail to Plead Sufficient Material Facts for Conspiracy,
Negligence or Breach of Fiduciary Duty

[
197
]

The defendants, EPL and Wanjin Yang, submit that
the conspiracy claim alleged against the defendants rests on the same wrongful
conduct which is alleged to constitute the alleged oppression under s. 227
of the
BCA
and is, therefore, also derivative. They point to the
decision of
Rogers v. Bank of Montreal,
9 B.C.L.R. (2d) 190,
1986 CanLII
847 (C.A.)
at paras.
5–6
, which held that due to the rule in
Foss v.
Harbottle

(1843), 2 Hare 461, 67 E.R. 189
,
a shareholder who suffers
a loss as a result of damage to a company cannot claim in conspiracy. This
decision was applied in
Robak Industries Ltd. v. Gardner,
2007 BCCA 61
[
Robak
]
at para.
35
, where the Court held:

[35]      There
are good reasons for not allowing a shareholder to claim the loss in value of
its shares where a wrong has been done to the company. As explained by Laskin
J.A. in
Meditrust
(at para. 13); La Forest J.
in
Hercules
(at para. 59), and McKenzie J.
in
Rogers
at 78-81 (citing
Prudential
Assurance
and
Green v. Victor Talking Mach. Co.
,
24
F. 2d 378
(1928) (C.A. 2nd Circ.)), the rule avoids a multiplicity of
actions. Further, and consistent with the legal theory of
Foss v.
Harbottle
, the loss in value of shares of a company is a loss of all of
the shareholders, not just one or some of them. There is no logic that would
allow only one shareholder to claim that loss, where the claim relates to
wrongs done to the company, and all of the shareholders have suffered the loss
in value. A single shareholder cannot claim that the loss in value of the
shares,
per se
, is a personal, direct loss.

[
198
]

The defendants, Ka An and Chang Yu Liu, adopt this submission but
also submit that taking the conspiracy pleadings on their face, they fail to
set out a reasonable cause of action for conspiracy. The defendants submit that
the conspiracy allegations largely rest on bald assumptions and speculation
that the Court is not obligated to take as true.

[
199
]

253 Ont. Ltd. submits that it has sufficiently pleaded the elements
of conspiracy and says that there is “no bright line between material facts and
bald allegations, nor between pleadings or material facts and the prohibition
on pleading of evidence”:
Teal Cedar Products Ltd. v. Rainforest Flying
Squad,
2023 BCSC 1821
at para.
11
.

[
200
]

Having reviewed the pleadings, I am satisfied that the allegations
of conspiracy pleaded in paras. 81–85 of the amended notice of civil claim to
the Oppression Action are not materially different from the allegations earlier
in the pleading that the Great Wall transactions were part of a broader scheme
to depreciate EPL’s share price and strip value out of EPL and, accordingly,
oppressive to the plaintiff. For the reasons articulated in
Robak
,
there
is no basis to allow 253 Ont. Ltd. to proceed with this action when it is based
on a loss to the company.

[
201
]

Given this conclusion, it is not necessary for me to address the
argument that there are no material facts pleaded to make out a claim in
conspiracy. However, the plaintiff has, in several respects, failed to
sufficiently particularize many of its allegations. A conspiracy claim is an
intentional tort and a serious allegation attracting a heightened requirement
of precision and clarity:
Gong
at para. 66. The Court of Appeal, in

H.M.B. Holdings
,
set out in detail what is required. This includes the
best particulars as to the defendant’s intent to injure the plaintiff which is
an essential element of the tort. With respect to this element, the pleadings
baldly claim, at paras. 54–56 of the amended notice of civil claim, that the
conduct of Mr. Liu, Ms. Liu, and Mr. Yang was “directed towards
the plaintiff” without providing any material facts to support that
conclusion.

[
202
]

Finally, the defendants argue that the plaintiff’s allegations that Mr. Yang
breached his duty of care and fiduciary duty cannot support a cause of action
for the plaintiff. The defendants rely on the fundamental corporate law
principle that directors and officers of a company owe a fiduciary duty only to
the company, not to its shareholders:
BCE Inc.
at para.
66
. There
are some exceptions to this rule when there is a family relationship or a
special relationship of trust and dependency between the parties where the
director seeks to take unfair advantage of others for personal gain or profit:
Yen
v. Ghahramani
,
2023 BCCA 403
at para.
69
. The defendants say that no
such special relationship is alleged. Further, these situations are more likely
to arise in closely-held corporations rather than a publicly traded corporation
like EPL.

[
203
]

In
Shon v. Argo Mezzanine Financing No. 3
Ltd.,
2014 BCSC 2117
at para.
71
, Justice Davies held, in reliance on
the Court of Appeal decision in
Robak
,
that for a shareholder to
establish a claim against a director of a company in either fiduciary duty or
negligence, both of the following elements must be established:

1)

an independent relationship between the shareholder and the director
as the alleged wrongdoer; and

2)

an independent loss suffered by the plaintiff, as a shareholder,
that is separate from the wrongs purportedly done by the director to the
company.

[
204
]

Mr. Hong points to the decision of
Craigmohr Holdings Ltd.
v. Baldassarre,
2022 BCSC 1984
, as standing for the proposition that
“directors have been found to owe a fiduciary duty towards other shareholders
in circumstances where the director seeks to take unfair advantage of others
for personal gain or profit.” However, this proposition is a fragment of the
narrow exception articulated by the Court of Appeal in
Yen
.
The complete
proposition requires that there be a special relationship of trust between the
plaintiff and the defendants. I agree with the defendants that no such
relationship is alleged in the plaintiff’s pleading. Further, as discussed
above, none of the losses alleged by the plaintiff are independent from losses
that would have been caused to EPL generally.

[
205
]

It is also apparent from the pleadings that no new or materially
different facts are pleaded to underpin the claims of fiduciary duty and
negligence than those pleaded in respect of the alleged oppressive conduct
which I have found is derivative in nature. Given that these derivative claims
cannot be brought without leave, permitting further amendments will not remedy
this defect.

[
206
]

Accordingly, the claims in fiduciary duty and negligence are bound
to fail and are, accordingly, struck.

Are the Great Wall Proceedings vexatious
and an abuse of process?

[
207
]

Finally, I turn to whether there are grounds to strike the Great
Wall Proceedings on the basis that they are vexatious and an abuse of the Court’s
process.

[
208
]

I agree with the defendants’ submissions the Great Wall Proceedings
bear many of the hallmarks of a vexatious proceeding. Despite Mr. Hong’s
insistence in his submissions that this action is based on new facts relating
to the Great Wall transaction, his pleadings continue to allege facts relating
to his failed takeover bid and loss of the proxy battle to Kan An, as well as
the Union Goal Transaction. Both of these matters were raised in the Oppression
Action, notwithstanding the Union Goal allegations was removed by consent.
Justice N. Smith also denied Mr. Hong leave to advance a derivative claim
with respect to the Union Goal Transaction.

[
209
]

Consistent with my findings in respect of the Oppression Action, I
have little difficulty in concluding that the repetitive Great Wall Proceedings
are being brought for an improper purpose to vex the defendants and are a
continuation of Mr. Hong’s campaign to seek retribution for his failed bid
to take over EPL. The fact that the plaintiff continues to seek orders in the
Great Wall Proceedings that Ka An sell its shares in EPL and that a new slate
of directors be elected supports the inference that Mr. Hong is still
seeking orders that would have the effect of accomplishing what Mr. Hong
failed to accomplish in the proxy battle.

[
210
]

As held by the Supreme Court of Canada in
BCE Inc.
at para.
43
,

the leave requirement for derivative actions is not a mere matter of form.
It is designed to prevent frivolous and vexatious actions and to ensure that
actions proposed are in the interests of the corporation to litigate. Given Mr. Hong’s
previous litigation experience in the 2018 Derivative Petition, it is
reasonable to presume that he is well-aware of this requirement. Despite this
knowledge, instead of seeking leave, he filed an unmeritorious claim for
oppression based on allegations of general damage to the company and its
shareholders in general.

[
211
]

In considering 253 Ont. Ltd.’s motivations in bringing the Great
Wall Proceedings, it is also relevant to consider the threats Mr. Hong made
in his letter dated April 10, 2024, prior to commencing the Great Wall Action. Mr. Hong
stated that if EPL did not prosecute a claim regarding the Great Wall
transactions, he would “seek leave to commence a derivative action pursuant to
the [
BCA
]”. In this request, Mr. Hong characterized the Great Wall
transactions as not being in the best interests of EPL. Despite this admission
that his concerns were properly remedied through a derivative claim, Mr. Hong
took the opposite approach and filed an oppression claim. Mr. Hong’s admissions
during submissions that filing a derivative proceeding would give him
insufficient control over the litigation, and that obtaining leave would be an
“uphill battle” in light of the Smith Decision, further suggests that the Great
Wall Action was commenced for ulterior motives rather than as a legitimate
means to seek a remedy for specific harms to 253 Ont. Ltd. The lack of material
facts within the pleadings to demonstrate that 253 Ont. Ltd. was affected differently
from the other shareholders of EPL by the Great Wall transactions further supports
this conclusion.

[
212
]

Finally, I note that the threat made by Mr. Hong in his April
10, 2024, letter to include two law firms advising EPL in its investigations of
the Great Wall allegations is a further indication of the vexatious nature of Mr. Hong’s
conduct:
Simon
at para. 97.

[
213
]

Accordingly, I exercise my discretion to strike the Great Wall Proceedings
in their entirety on the basis that they constitute an abuse of process.

Conclusion

[
214
]

As the successful parties on these applications, the defendants are
entitled to their costs. They are also entitled to their costs of the
application before Sharma J. who deferred the determination of costs of the
stay application to the judge hearing the strike applications.

[
215
]

In their notices of application in both the oppression action and
the Great Wall Proceedings, Ka An and Chang Yu Liu seek special costs. EPL and
Wanjin Yang seek special costs only in its notice of application in the Great
Wall Proceeding. Ms. Hu did not seek special costs in her notice of
application.

[
216
]

Special costs are generally awarded against a party that has engaged
in some form of reprehensible conduct in the course of the litigation:
Gichuru
v. Pallai
,
2018 BCCA 78
at para.
86
. If granted, special costs
entitle a party to have their costs assessed either as a complete or partial
indemnity of the actual legal costs incurred:
Kyle Estate v. Kyle,
2017
BCCA 329
at para.
45
. Given their punitive nature, procedural fairness
demands that a party against who special costs should be made aware of the
claim against it and be given an opportunity to respond to it:
Gichuru

at para.
88
.

[
217
]

In my view, such an opportunity was not afforded to Mr. Hong
and 253 Ont. Ltd. Insufficient court time was scheduled for the hearing of this
application which took four full days to be heard, despite being scheduled for three
days. Even with the additional day added to the hearing, very little of the
defendants’ submissions spoke to the issue of costs. Further, the defendants’
written submissions did not elaborate on their request for special costs.

[
218
]

In these circumstances, I decline to order
special costs. The defendants are entitled to costs at Scale B against Mr. Hong
and 253 Ont. Ltd. in Action S201427, and against 253 Ont. Ltd. in S244818 and
S252308.

“Hoffman
J.”
